transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moran (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jonas Li (Redwood SE), Ben Park (CTO - Lyra), Sara Gomez (ML Eng), Derek Wu (Platform), Maya Ortiz (PM)

Summary:
Quick POC-scoping focused on defining latency/throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), workload sizing, and a concrete benchmark & measurement plan. Agreed on initial targets and next steps to run warm/cold benchmarks on Redwood Dedicated and report p95/p99.

Topics (auto): TTFT definitions, TPOT modelling, p95/p99 targets by payload class, benchmark harness, KV/prefix caching, timeline for runs.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Moran: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — Alex from Redwood, Priya and Jonas from our SE team. Ben, do you want to kick off with a little context on what Lyra's trying to validate in the POC?

[00:15] Ben Park: Yeah thanks. So, high level, Lyra is embedding an assistant in our support product. Typical request is short chat-style queries, plus some longer summarization jobs. The thing we need to lock down is latency under production traffic — both the time to first token, which matters for perceived responsiveness in chat, and then the per-token throughput for longer responses. We want SLOs and a measurement plan to validate Dedicated vs Hosted.

[00:40] Maya Ortiz: Timeline wise we want to be able to decide by end of month if we go Dedicated for Q3. So the POC needs to be quick.

[00:48] Priya Shah: Great — that's tight but doable. Quick clarification on terms so we're aligned: we usually separate TTFT (time-to-first-token) — that's everything up to the model producing the first token — and TPOT which our customers shorthand for time-per-output-token or steady-state per-token latency. Do you use the same definitions?

[01:10] Sara Gomez: Yes, that's how we think about it. Example: small chat replies ~20-80 tokens, quick TTFT is critical, while longer summarizations 200-600 tokens are dominated by TPOT.

[01:30] Jonas Li: Cool. For scoping, we usually break the workload into classes. We suggested three classes in the doc I shared:
- Class A: short chat replies (<=64 tokens) — latency-sensitive, low token counts.
- Class B: medium responses (65-256 tokens) — mixed sensitivity.
- Class C: long generations (257-1024 tokens) — bulk throughput matters more.

[01:50] Derek Wu: Our current numbers — at peak we see 120 QPS of chat queries, median seq length around 48 tokens, 95th token-length ~150. Concurrency tops at roughly 60 concurrent open requests.

[02:05] Alex Moran: That helps a lot. For an initial POC we typically recommend testing at target QPS of 1.5x to 2x current peak to validate headroom. So for you that'd be ~180-240 QPS. Sound reasonable?

[02:18] Ben Park: Yes, let's do 2x.

[02:22] Priya Shah: Ok, SLO proposals — we suggest two sets: conservative (baseline for Hosted) and aggressive (target if Dedicated + optimized kernels + caching). Rough initial targets:
- TTFT (Class A): Hosted p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 450ms; Dedicated p95 <= 150ms, p99 <= 300ms.
- TPOT (Class A small tokens): p95 <= 25ms/token, p99 <= 45ms/token.
- For Class B/C (longer): TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token and p99 <= 60ms/token, but this scales with sequence length and model variant.

[03:05] Sara Gomez: Those numbers seem in the right ballpark. Why the big difference in TTFT between Hosted and Dedicated?

[03:10] Priya Shah: A few reasons — Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity and more predictable kernel placement. Also Dedicated allows more aggressive batching and hotter KV caches for prompt prefixes. Hosted has multi-tenant routing variability and occasional cold-start tail events. We can also tune kernel selection and quantization on Dedicated.

[03:40] Ben Park: Ok. How do you plan to measure TTFT precisely? Our monitoring team needs concrete instrumentation.

[03:48] Jonas Li: Measurement approach — we'll instrument at three points: client request timestamp, Redwood ingress time, and model token-emission timestamp (first token). Our benchmark harness will capture per-request traces and compute TTFT, TPOT per-token, and aggregate percentiles (p50/p95/p99). We'll also capture CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, and batching stats.

[04:15] Derek Wu: Are you measuring cold-starts? We see a lot of user sessions with infrequent prompts, so cold behavior matters.

[04:22] Priya Shah: Yes. We'll run both cold and warm tests. Cold tests start from an idle cluster (we'll restart or scale-to-zero if possible) and measure the worst-case tails. Warm tests simulate steady-state with KV cache primed and steady request streams. We'll also test cache priming strategies — prefix caching and session KV warmup.

[04:45] Sara Gomez: For the p99 tails, do you include network latency or is it pure server-side?

[04:52] Alex Moran: We'll provide both. Our internal perf harness reports server-side latencies (ingress to first-token) and we can also report end-to-end from a simulated client host in your region to include network. For acceptance criteria we recommend using server-side latencies to decouple network noise.

[05:10] Ben Park: OK good. What about measurement windows? We need to ensure the percentiles are stable.

[05:16] Jonas Li: We suggest running each test for at least 30 minutes after steady-state is reached. For percentile stability at p99, longer windows are better — 1 hour preferred for final validation. We'll run 3 iterations and report median result plus variation.

[05:33] Priya Shah: Also important — we will run tests across model variants (e.g., quantized vs fp16), different sequence lengths, and different concurrency shapes (spiky vs steady).

[05:44] Maya Ortiz: On tooling — what do you use? Our infra team prefers open tools.

[05:48] Priya Shah: We typically use a combination: Locust for synthetic traffic shaping, a small custom harness that hits Redwood endpoints and collects per-token timestamps, and GPU telemetry via Prometheus + nvidia-smi exporters. We'll hand you docker images so you can run locally or let us run them from our infra.

[06:05] Derek Wu: We prefer you run from inside our VPC for Dedicated tests so we get true network numbers. Can Redwood run inside our VPC?

[06:12] Alex Moran: Yes, for Redwood Private/Dedicated we can work inside your VPC or run from a test host in your cloud region. We'll coordinate network setup in the POC onboarding doc.

[06:24] Ben Park: Back to SLO numbers — can you provide an example acceptance matrix we can sign off on?

[06:30] Priya Shah: Sure. Example matrix we propose in the doc:
- Class A (<=64 tokens) at 2x peak (240 QPS):
  - TTFT p95 <= 150ms (Dedicated), p99 <= 300ms
  - TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token, TPOT p99 <= 45ms/token
- Class B (65-256 tokens) at mixed load:
  - TTFT less strict: p95 <= 250ms
  - TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token
- Class C (>=257 tokens):
  - Focus on throughput: sustained token/sec per GPU numbers and end-to-end p95 p99 for full generation within acceptable window (e.g., 90th percentile total generation time < 4s for 512-token outputs)

[07:15] Sara Gomez: For Class C that 4s target seems aggressive for 512 tokens unless TPOT is ~8ms/token; is that realistic?

[07:22] Jonas Li: Agreed that 8ms/token is aggressive. We're suggesting instead to measure token throughput and then map to user-visible targets. For example, if TPOT ~20-25ms/token, a 512-token generation would be ~10-12s. For UX we recommend streaming partial responses early to hide tail.

[07:42] Ben Park: That makes sense, so for long jobs we care more about cost per token and acceptable UX patterns (streaming).

[07:50] Priya Shah: Exactly. Also mention that batching behavior can add TTFT tail when batch windows increase. We will capture batching histograms — avg batch size and max.

[08:02] Derek Wu: About caching — how much speedup do you typically see from KV/prefix cache on short chats?

[08:08] Priya Shah: For repeated prefixes or instruction-heavy prompts, KV cache can reduce total token generation significantly; TTFT sees modest benefit (since first-token still needs some model work) but TPOT for subsequent tokens is much faster because KV cache reduces attention/memory ops. On average we've seen 20-40% effective per-token latency reduction for workloads with good prefix reuse. But it depends on sessionization.

[08:35] Ben Park: Ok useful. For the POC acceptance, can we include both cold-start guarantees and warm steady-state guarantees?

[08:42] Alex Moran: Absolutely. Proposed acceptance criteria: pass both warm-run SLOs (as above) at 2x peak, and cold-run p95 within 2x warm p95 (i.e., cold p95 not catastrophically worse). If cold p99 is large, we can document mitigation (keep-hot or pre-warm).

[09:00] Maya Ortiz: Deployment constraints: we need SOC2 audit logs, SSO/SAML integration, and KMS key control. This will affect how quickly we can spin up Dedicated.

[09:09] Alex Moran: Noted — we'll include a security package and timeline for SSO/KMS setup. That usually takes a week for initial config with your security team.

[09:20] Ben Park: On reporting, we want a short dashboard with p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, plus GPU util, batch sizes, and error rates. Can you deliver that?

[09:29] Jonas Li: Yes — we'll generate a per-route dashboard in the Redwood Console and provide CSV exports and the raw traces.

[09:36] Sara Gomez: Regarding model variants — we may test two models: a smaller quantized model for cheap chat and a larger high-quality model for long summaries. Will that complicate benchmarking?

[09:45] Priya Shah: We'll treat them as separate test vectors. For each variant we'll run the same matrix (Class A/B/C) and report cost/latency tradeoffs. That will help you decide which workloads map to which model and whether to route by policy.

[10:00] Ben Park: Great. One more operational question — what's the suggested duration for the POC itself? We want enough time to iterate and validate.

[10:07] Alex Moran: Typical POC is 3-4 weeks: week 1 onboarding and test setup, week 2 run initial benchmarks and iterate tuning, week 3 final validation and report. If security integrations add time we'll extend. You said you want decision by end of May — that's tight but possible if we start immediately.

[10:24] Maya Ortiz: Ok let's target a compressed 3-week POC starting next Monday.

[10:30] Priya Shah: Action items recap — we'll share the benchmark scripts, you share traffic sample, we'll schedule Dedicated runs inside your VPC, and we'll produce the acceptance matrix and final report.

[10:40] Ben Park: Sounds good. Quick technical note — please capture queueing latency separately from model compute time; our infra SLOs care about queueing.

[10:48] Jonas Li: Yes, our harness logs queue time, compute time, and emission time per-request.

[10:55] Sara Gomez: And please include guidance on batching windows/limits; we want to avoid latency spikes from large automatic batches.

[11:03] Priya Shah: We'll include recommended batching configs (max batch latency thresholds, max batch size by model).

[11:10] Derek Wu: For measuring p99 reliably, do you recommend synthetic noise injection (like occasional slow nodes) to simulate noisy infra?

[11:18] Alex Moran: We can simulate noisy nodes but we recommend starting with clean runs to baseline then a resilience test where we throttle one node or add latency to emulate network blips. We'll capture fallbacks and routing behavior.

[11:32] Ben Park: Cool. Anything else?

[11:36] Maya Ortiz: No, that's it from product.

[11:38] Alex Moran: Alright great — recap and next steps: Alex will send POC proposal and pricing by Friday, Priya will share the benchmark harness and docker images by Wednesday, and Derek will upload an anonymized traffic sample by Thursday. We'll target the first Redwood-run benchmarks the week of 2026-05-18 and aim to have a results report within 48 hours of each run.

[11:58] Ben Park: Thanks everyone.

[12:00] Meeting end.
